h1:
Bangkok Attractions
15 Spots Worth Your Time
intro: Bangkok lets you travel in several modes in a single city: temple-hop through the old town in the morning, browse a market or riverside mall in the afternoon, then cycle through the green lung of Bang Krachao in the evening. We picked 15 spots that people actually go to and that pay off for the time you spend, split into culture, city and nature, with entry fees and opening hours we checked for 2026.

blocks.html: If it's your first time in Bangkok, the first question is usually "where do I even go," because there's so much that picking feels impossible. The easiest way is to split things by zone and by theme, then do one theme per day so you don't burn out. Most of the temple sights sit in the old Rattanakosin quarter and are walkable from each other. The city stuff clusters around Siam–Ratchaprasong and along the Chao Phraya River, while the nature spots are a little outside the centre but not far.

blocks.text: Culture: Temples and the Old Town

blocks.html: Bangkok's three main temples are right next to each other in the Rattanakosin quarter. Go in the morning before the sun gets harsh and the crowds build. You can walk from the Grand Palace to Wat Pho, and Wat Arun is just a few minutes across the river on the Thonburi side. Every temple has a dress code: no tank tops, no shorts above the knee, and nothing sheer or see-through.

items.name: Grand Palace + Wat Phra Kaew
items.blurb: The city's number-one landmark, home to the Emerald Buddha and full-on Thai architecture. Foreigner ticket is 500 THB and includes the Queen Sirikit Museum of Textiles, valid for 7 days. Open 8:30–15:30. Strict dress code.

items.name: Wat Pho (Wat Phra Chetuphon)
items.blurb: Home to the giant 46-metre Reclining Buddha and the birthplace of Thai massage. Walkable from Wat Phra Kaew. Entry 300 THB (includes one bottle of water). Open 8:00–18:30.

items.name: Wat Arun (Temple of Dawn)
items.blurb: The riverside prang on the Chao Phraya, lovely by day and when it's lit up at night. A few minutes by ferry from Tha Tien pier. Entry 200 THB. Open 8:00–18:00. You can currently climb up to the first level of the prang.

items.name: Golden Mount (Wat Saket)
items.blurb: Climb roughly 300 spiral steps to the golden chedi and a 360-degree view over the old town. Great for sunset. Foreigner entry around 50 THB, free for Thais. Open 7:00–19:00.

items.name: Jim Thompson House Museum
items.blurb: A teak Thai house set in a garden in the centre near Siam, telling the story of Thai silk and the mystery of its owner's disappearance. A guided tour is included with the ticket. Adult entry 200 THB, students under 22 pay 100 THB. Open 10:00–17:00.

blocks.title: Temple tip
blocks.html: Watch out for people who claim "the temple is closed today" and then try to talk you into a tuk-tuk tour that ends at a gem shop. The main temples open on their normal hours almost every day. Just walk to the official entrance and check for yourself.

blocks.title: Want more out of Bangkok? Book tours & activities
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Bangkok
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.text: City: Markets, Malls and the River

blocks.html: The other side of Bangkok is a city that never sleeps. Around Siam–Ratchaprasong you can mall-hop along the connected skywalk, while the Chao Phraya riverside has both luxury malls and night markets. If you're into vintage finds and crafts, Chatuchak is the place.

items.name: Chatuchak Weekend Market
items.blurb: One of the largest weekend markets in the world, with over 15,000 stalls selling clothes, home decor, antiques and plants. Open Sat–Sun 9:00–18:00 (some sections Wed–Thu). Next to BTS Mo Chit / MRT Chatuchak.

items.name: ICONSIAM
items.blurb: A riverside mall on the Thonburi side, with the indoor floating-market zone SOOKSIAM selling food from across Thailand. Head up to floor 7 for a free river view, with a fountain show in the evening. Free shuttle boat from Sathorn pier.

items.name: Asiatique The Riverfront
items.blurb: A riverside night market in old warehouses, with a Ferris wheel, waterfront restaurants and shows. Open evening to late. Free shuttle boat from Sathorn pier. Good for catching the sunset.

items.name: Siam–Ratchaprasong Area
items.blurb: The hub of big malls: Siam Paragon, CentralWorld and MBK, all linked by skywalk. The Erawan Shrine is here too if you want to stop and pay respects. Next to BTS Siam / Chit Lom.

items.name: Talat Noi–Yaowarat
items.blurb: The old quarter on the Chinatown side, with classic shophouses, street art, little cafes and food running the length of Yaowarat Road after dark. Good for wandering and photos all day.

blocks.text: Nature: Green Spaces in the City

blocks.html: Bangkok has more green lungs than you'd think, from free city parks to Bang Krachao island on the Samut Prakan side, where you can cycle through gardens all day. It's a good way to take a break from the chaos without leaving town.

items.name: Lumphini Park
items.blurb: A central park next to Silom–Sathorn, free to enter, open 4:30–21:00. There's a lake you can paddle on, monitor lizards you'll often spot, and runners and exercisers morning and evening. Next to MRT Silom / Lumphini.

items.name: Bang Krachao
items.blurb: Bangkok's green lung on the Samut Prakan side. Cycle along the canals past gardens and orchards. Bike rental is around 100 THB/day, and the cross-river ferry from Khlong Toei is just a few THB. Bang Nam Phueng floating market is open Sat–Sun 7:00–15:00.

items.name: Benjakitti Park
items.blurb: A forest park in the city behind the Sirikit Convention Center, with an elevated walkway through woods and wetlands. Free to enter, good for an evening stroll and photos. Linked to Lumphini Park by skywalk. Next to MRT Queen Sirikit National Convention Centre.

blocks.title: Green-space tip
blocks.html: Bang Krachao is most fun in the early morning before it gets late and hot, when it's shadier and the air is better. Go on a Saturday or Sunday and you can stop at the Bang Nam Phueng floating market too. Bring cash, since plenty of stalls still don't take transfers.

blocks.text: How to Plan Your Days Without Burning Out

blocks.html: If you have 2–3 days, doing one theme per day is more enjoyable than cramming everything into one. Here's a short plan with stops that actually flow together.

items.activity: Start at the Grand Palace + Wat Phra Kaew
items.note: Go early to beat the sun and crowds; dress modestly

items.activity: Walk on to Wat Pho to see the Reclining Buddha
items.note: You can try a Thai massage inside the temple

items.activity: Eat around Tha Tien, then take the ferry to Wat Arun
items.note: The cross-river ferry costs just a few THB

items.activity: Finish at the Golden Mount for sunset
Stop by the Jim Thompson House
items.note: Guided tour included with the ticket

items.activity: Take the free boat from Sathorn pier to ICONSIAM
items.note: Head up to floor 7 for the river view

items.activity: Carry on to Asiatique for the lights and a riverside dinner
items.note: There's a Ferris wheel for photos

items.activity: Take the ferry across to cycle Bang Krachao
Stop at Bang Nam Phueng floating market (Sat–Sun)
Head back into town and stroll Benjakitti Park
End the trip at Lumphini Park in the evening

items: BTS/MRT — the fastest way and the best for dodging traffic, covering Siam, Chatuchak, Silom and Sukhumvit. A stored-value card is more convenient.
Chao Phraya Express Boat — board at Sathorn pier (linked to BTS Saphan Taksin) and reach Wat Arun, Wat Pho and ICONSIAM all on one line.
Taxi / ride-hailing app — booking through an app is convenient and runs on the meter, so you avoid haggling. Steer clear of the morning and evening rush hours.
Walking — in the old Rattanakosin quarter several temples are walkable from each other. Carry an umbrella or a sun hat.

faq.q: What are the must-see Bangkok attractions for a first visit?
faq.a: The three old-town temples — the Grand Palace with Wat Phra Kaew, Wat Pho and Wat Arun — are the set most first-timers don't skip. All three are close together and you can do them back-to-back in half a day. If you want both the city and nature, add Chatuchak, ICONSIAM and either Lumphini Park or Bang Krachao.

faq.q: How much are Bangkok temple entry fees in 2026?
faq.a: Grand Palace + Wat Phra Kaew is 500 THB for foreigners, Wat Pho is 300 THB, Wat Arun is 200 THB, and the Golden Mount at Wat Saket is around 50 THB. Thais get in free or pay less at many temples.

faq.q: What nature spots are there in Bangkok?
faq.a: In the city you have Lumphini Park and Benjakitti Park, both free to enter and walkable from each other via skywalk. If you want to cycle in proper nature, cross over to Bang Krachao on the Samut Prakan side, where bike rental is around 100 THB a day.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Bangkok?
faq.a: Two to three days is just right for the main sights without rushing, doing one theme per day: temples on day one, the city and river on day two, nature on day three. If you have more time, add a day trip to Ayutthaya or Samut Songkhram.

faq.q: What days is Chatuchak Market open?
faq.a: The main sections are open Sat–Sun 9:00–18:00, with some sections open Wed–Thu and on Friday night too. Go in the morning or late afternoon, since midday is hot and packed. Next to BTS Mo Chit or MRT Chatuchak.
